claims.source: Located between the N-terminal signal peptide and the TM1, LD is a~110 amino acids long β-sandwich made of two beta sheets of four strands each where strands β1, β4, β7, & β8 form the mixed β-sheet on top (Figure 1A–E, blue), and the strands β2, β3, β5, & β6 arrange as bottom anti-parallel β-sheet (Figure 1A–E, gray).
claims.evidence: This describes the strand arrangement in the LD structure.

claims.claim: Strands β2, β3, β5, & β6 arrange as bottom anti-parallel β-sheet of the LD.
claims.source: Located between the N-terminal signal peptide and the TM1, LD is a~110 amino acids long β-sandwich made of two beta sheets of four strands each where strands β1, β4, β7, & β8 form the mixed β-sheet on top (Figure 1A–E, blue), and the strands β2, β3, β5, & β6 arrange as bottom anti-parallel β-sheet (Figure 1A–E, gray).
claims.evidence: This describes the strand arrangement in the LD structure.

claims.claim: The mixed β-sheet is arranged such that the order of the strands is β4-β1-β7-β8, with β1 & β7 being parallel.
claims.source: The mixed β-sheet is arranged such that the order of the strands is β4-β1-β7-β8, with β1 & β7 being parallel.
claims.evidence: This describes the detailed arrangement of strands in the mixed β-sheet.

claims.claim: β8 of LD is connected to TM1.
claims.source: β8 of LD is connected to TM1 (Figures 1B, D, 2A).
claims.evidence: This describes the connectivity between LD and TMD.

claims.claim: LD has two predicted disulfide bonds – one in the β-turn that connects β2 and β3 (C76-C79), and the other between the strands β6 and β8 (C123-C151).
claims.source: LD has two predicted disulfide bonds – one in the β-turn that connects β2 and β3 (C76-C79), and the other between the strands β6 and β8 (C123-C151) holding the two sheets together.
claims.evidence: This describes predicted disulfide bonds based on cysteine positions.

claims.claim: The resolution of the LD domain allows unambiguous modeling of only one disulfide bond (C76-C79).
claims.source: The resolution of the LD domain in our structure allows us to model only one (C76-C79) of these unambiguously (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This describes a limitation of the structural data.

claims.claim: HGSNAT is produced as a pro-protein that is believed to get proteolyzed into two fragments, HGSNAT-α and HGSNAT-β, of unequal sizes, which remain together.
claims.source: HGSNAT is produced as a pro-protein that is believed to get proteolyzed into two fragments, HGSNAT-α and HGSNAT-β, of unequal sizes, which remain together (Durand et al., 2010; Fan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This describes the biosynthesis of HGSNAT, supported by citations.

claims.claim: It is unclear if HGSNAT-α is made of just LD or LD and TM1, and if HGSNAT-β is made of all TMs or only TMs2-11.
claims.source: It is unclear if HGSNAT-α is made of just LD or LD and TM1, and if HGSNAT-β is made of all TMs or only TMs2-11 (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes uncertainty about the exact boundaries of the proteolytic fragments.

claims.claim: The FSEC and SDS-PAGE analyses of the purified protein indicate that the recombinant HGSNAT is not proteolyzed.
claims.source: While our structure has relatively poor local resolution at the predicted protease sites, making it difficult to map them unambiguously, the FSEC nor the SDS-PAGE analyses of the purified protein indicate that the recombinant HGSNAT is not proteolyzed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claims.claim: The relatively low local resolution of LD is because of the flexibility introduced by GFP fused to the N-term of HGSNAT.
claims.source: We believe the relatively low local resolution of LD is because of the flexibility introduced by GFP fused to the N-term of HGSNAT.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of poor resolution in the LD.

claims.claim: LD interacts with TMD at multiple sites via an extensive interaction network that spans ~35 Å, comprised of a salt bridge (D52-H605), hydrogen bonds, and dipole-dipole and hydrophobic interactions.
claims.source: LD interacts with TMD at multiple sites via an extensive interaction network that spans ~35 Å, comprised of a salt bridge (D52-H605), hydrogen bonds, and dipole-dipole and hydrophobic interactions (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This describes the LD-TMD interface observed in the structure.

claims.claim: The N-terminus of TM11 interacts with the N-terminus of β1 and LL1.
claims.source: The N-terminus of TM11 interacts with the N-terminus of β1 and LL1.
claims.evidence: This describes specific interactions at the LD-TMD interface.

claims.claim: LL1 also interacts with the N-terminus of TM1 and the β4-β5 turn.
claims.source: LL1 also interacts with the N-terminus of TM1 and the β4-β5 turn.
claims.evidence: This describes specific interactions at the LD-TMD interface.

claims.claim: The β2-β3 turn, including the C76-C79 disulfide, interacts extensively with LL3 and is a part of LL4.
claims.source: The β2-β3 turn, including the C76-C79 disulfide, interacts extensively with LL3 and is a part of LL4.
claims.evidence: This describes specific interactions at the LD-TMD interface.

claims.claim: The β2-β3 turn-LL3-LL4 interaction is stabilized by a 3π-network formed by the stacking of Y77, H78, & F428 side chains.
claims.source: The β2-β3 turn-LL3-LL4 interaction is also stabilized by a 3π-network formed by the stacking of Y77, H78, & F428 side chains.
claims.evidence: This describes a specific stabilizing interaction at the LD-TMD interface.

claims.claim: The hydrogen bond network that stabilizes the LD-TMD interaction is formed between the amino acids M51, H78, and S162 of LD with H605 and Q603, D427 and F428, and Y264 of the TMD, respectively.
claims.source: The hydrogen bond network that stabilizes the LD-TMD interaction is formed between the amino acids M51, H78, and S162 of LD with H605 and Q603, D427 and F428, and Y264 of the TMD, respectively (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This describes specific hydrogen bonds at the LD-TMD interface.

claims.claim: The LD-TMD interface is separated from the dimer interface by the central catalytic core.
claims.source: The LD-TMD interface is separated from the dimer interface by the central catalytic core (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This describes the spatial relationship between different interfaces.

claims.claim: The dimer interface is spread across ~35 Å towards the luminal side of the protein, perpendicular to the C2 rotation axis.
claims.source: The dimer interface is spread across ~35 Å towards the luminal side of the protein, perpendicular to the C2 rotation axis (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This describes the extent and orientation of the dimer interface.

claims.claim: Although TMs 4, 10, and 11 from both protomers lie on either side of the dimer interface, they do not directly interact to stabilize the dimer interface.
claims.source: Although the TMs 4, 10, and 11 from both protomers lie on either side of the dimer interface, they do not directly interact to stabilize the dimer interface.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about which TMs are not involved in dimerization.

claims.claim: The primary mediator of dimerization is the disulfide between C334s within the LL2s of each protomer.
claims.source: The primary mediator of dimerization is the disulfide between C334s within the LL2s of each protomer (Figure 2C, rectangle inset).
claims.evidence: This describes the main interaction stabilizing the dimer.

claims.claim: In addition to the C334-C334 disulfide, the dimer interface is also stabilized by an extensive π-π interaction network formed between the aromatic residues of LL2 (332-340) of one protomer and the aromatic residues of LL5 (588-598) of the other protomer.
claims.source: In addition to the C334-C334 disulfide, the dimer interface is also stabilized by an extensiveπ-π interaction network formed between the aromatic residues of LL2 (332-340) of one protomer and the aromatic residues of LL5 (588-598) of the other protomer (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This describes additional interactions stabilizing the dimer interface.

claims.claim: The aromatic bulky side chains at the dimer interface are buried in the membrane, and the hydrophilic residues face the lumen.
claims.source: Notably, the aromatic bulky side chains at the interface are buried in the membrane, and the hydrophilic residues face the lumen (Figure 2C, oval inset).
claims.evidence: This describes the orientation of residues at the dimer interface.

claims.claim: Y333, L338, and S339 of LL2 from one protomer form a series of hydrogen bonds with F593 and K598 of LL5 of the other protomer.
claims.source: Y333, L338, and S339 of LL2 from one protomer form a series of hydrogen bonds with F593 and K598 of LL5 of the other protomer, which adds to the stabilization of the dimer interface (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This describes specific hydrogen bonds at the dimer interface.

claims.claim: In all the detergents tested, HGSNAT eluted as a dimer.
claims.source: In all the detergents we tested, HGSNAT eluted as a dimer, a testimony to the extensive side-chain interaction network.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation supporting the stability of the dimer.

claims.claim: The twofold rotational symmetry between the protomers juxtaposes the ACOSs of protomers connecting them with each other on the cytosolic side.
claims.source: The twofold rotational symmetry between the protomers juxtaposes the ACOSs of protomers connecting them with each other on the cytosolic side (Figures 1 and 2C).
claims.evidence: This describes the spatial relationship between active sites in the dimer.

claims.claim: The interconnected space between ACOSs is partitioned by lipids, preventing the diffusion of ligands from one active site to the other within a dimer.
claims.source: This interconnected space is partitioned by lipids, preventing the diffusion of ligands from one active site to the other within a dimer (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the structure showing ordered lipid density.

claims.claim: The authors generated two HGSNAT mutants of residues at the dimer interface – C334A and F593A.
claims.source: We generated two HGSNAT mutants of residues at the dimer interface – C334A and F593A.
claims.evidence: This describes experimental work to test the importance of dimer interface residues.

claims.claim: In both C334A and F593A mutants, the overall expression of HGSNAT was not reduced.
claims.source: In both these mutants, the overall expression of HGSNAT was not reduced.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation about mutant expression levels.

claims.claim: In the F593A mutant, the stability of the dimer remained unaffected.
claims.source: In the case of F593A, the stability of the dimer also remained unaffected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,H,I and N).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation about the F593A mutant.

claims.claim: Both C334A and F593A mutants still expressed predominantly as dimers even in the presence of 1% digitonin.
claims.source: While both these mutants still expressed predominantly as dimers even in the presence of 1% digitonin, the C334A mutant eluted as a monomer upon heat treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,H,I and K).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation about the oligomeric state of mutants.

claims.claim: The C334A mutant eluted as a monomer upon heat treatment.
claims.source: While both these mutants still expressed predominantly as dimers even in the presence of 1% digitonin, the C334A mutant eluted as a monomer upon heat treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,H,I and K).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation showing the effect of breaking the disulfide bond.

claims.claim: In the absence of the C334-C334 disulfide, the extensive side-chain interaction network stabilizes the dimer interface at room temperature, but heating destabilizes these interactions, resulting in a monomeric C334A.
claims.source: As C334A breaks a covalent disulfide link between the protomers, in the absence of this disulfide, the extensive side-chain interaction network stabilizes the dimer interface. Heating destabilizes these interactions, resulting in a monomeric C334A.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results for the C334A mutant.

claims.claim: MOLEonline predicted the presence of a ~75 Å pore within the TMD, that begins at the cytosolic side and extends to the luminal side.
claims.source: We used MOLEonline to predict the presence of a~75 Å pore within the TMD, that begins at the cytosolic side and extends to the luminal side (Pravda et al., 2018; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This describes a computational prediction using the structure.

claims.claim: The pore predicted by MOLEonline is lined by highly conserved residues of TMs 2–5 and TM 10.
claims.source: The pore predicted by MOLEonline is lined by highly conserved residues of the TMs 2–5 and TM 10 (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This combines computational prediction with conservation analysis.

claims.claim: The helix TM10 is bent by ~80° such that the luminal-side 2/3rd (TM10b) of the helix is parallel to TM2 and the cytosolic-side 1/3rd (TM10a) of the helix protrudes between TM2 and TM11.
claims.source: We note that the helix TM10 is bent by ~80o such that the luminal-side 2/3rd (TM10b) of the helix is parallel to TM2 and the cytosolic-side 1/3rd (TM10a) of the helix protrudes between TM2 and TM11 (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This describes a structural feature of TM10.

claims.claim: The bending of TM10 is aided by P575 and G576, residues known to induce helix breaks and kinks.
claims.source: The bending of TM10 is aided by P575 and G576, residues are known to induce helix breaks and kinks (Javadpour et al., 1999; Ulmschneider and Sansom, 2001).
claims.evidence: This explains the structural basis for TM10 bending, supported by citations about proline and glycine effects on helices.

claims.claim: The authors found density in the cryo-EM map overlapping the MOLEonline prediction in both protomers, spanning the entire length of TMD, that allowed unambiguous modeling of a single acetyl-CoA.
claims.source: We find a density in our cryo-EM map overlapping the MOLEonline prediction in both protomers, spanning the entire length of TMD, that allowed us to unambiguously model a single acetyl-CoA, such that the 3', 5'-ADP nucleoside head group is towards the cytosol and the acetyl group is hydrogen bonded (~3.5 Å) to N258 of TM2 that is located at the luminal entrance of ACOS.
claims.evidence: This describes the identification and modeling of acetyl-CoA in the structure.

claims.claim: In the HGSNAT structure, the 3', 5'-ADP nucleoside head group of acetyl-CoA is towards the cytosol and the acetyl group is hydrogen bonded (~3.5 Å) to N258 of TM2.
claims.source: We find a density in our cryo-EM map overlapping the MOLEonline prediction in both protomers, spanning the entire length of TMD, that allowed us to unambiguously model a single acetyl-CoA, such that the 3', 5'-ADP nucleoside head group is towards the cytosol and the acetyl group is hydrogen bonded (~3.5 Å) to N258 of TM2 that is located at the luminal entrance of ACOS.
claims.evidence: This describes the orientation and interactions of acetyl-CoA in the structure.

claims.claim: The catalytic H269 is ~4.5 Å away from the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA.
claims.source: The catalytic H269, which is predicted to be acetylated during the acetyltransferase reaction, is ~4.5 Å away from the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA, nestled within the negative charge on the luminal opening, and is ergonomically positioned to perform acetyltransferase reaction in the presence of the acetyl group acceptor (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This describes the position of the catalytic residue relative to the substrate.

claims.claim: H269 is predicted to be acetylated during the acetyltransferase reaction.
claims.source: The catalytic H269, which is predicted to be acetylated during the acetyltransferase reaction, is ~4.5 Å away from the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA, nestled within the negative charge on the luminal opening, and is ergonomically positioned to perform acetyltransferase reaction in the presence of the acetyl group acceptor (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on prior biochemical studies cited earlier in the manuscript.

claims.claim: H269 is ergonomically positioned to perform acetyltransferase reaction in the presence of the acetyl group acceptor.
claims.source: The catalytic H269, which is predicted to be acetylated during the acetyltransferase reaction, is ~4.5 Å away from the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA, nestled within the negative charge on the luminal opening, and is ergonomically positioned to perform acetyltransferase reaction in the presence of the acetyl group acceptor (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural positioning of H269.

claims.claim: The binding pocket shows a polarity of charge, changing from positive to neutral to negative as one moves from the cytosolic side to the luminal side.
claims.source: The binding pocket, like the rest of the protein, shows a polarity of charge. As we move from the cytosolic side to the luminal side, the charge changes from positive to neutral to negative (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and D).
claims.evidence: This describes the electrostatic properties of the binding pocket.

claims.claim: The cytosolic opening of the ACOS is comprised of basic and nonpolar amino acids, making it an ideal pocket for binding the 3', 5'-ADP head group.
claims.source: The cytosolic opening of the site is comprised of basic and nonpolar amino acids, making it an ideal pocket for binding the 3', 5'-ADP head group.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the chemical complementarity between the pocket and the ligand.

claims.claim: The pantothenate group of acetyl-CoA is supported by a network of nonpolar amino acids at the center of the binding pocket.
claims.source: The pantothenate group of acetyl-CoA is supported by a network of nonpolar amino acids at the center of the binding pocket (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and D).
claims.evidence: This describes interactions between acetyl-CoA and the protein.

claims.claim: A series of conserved salt bridges stabilize the cytosolic and luminal entrances of the pore.
claims.source: A series of conserved salt bridges stabilize the cytosolic and luminal entrances of the pore.
claims.evidence: This describes structural features that stabilize the active site.

claims.claim: The luminal entrance is lined with salt bridges between the residues H269, D279, R344, D469, E471, H586, and E587.
claims.source: The luminal entrance is lined with salt bridges between the residues H269, D279, R344, D469, E471, H586, and E587.
claims.evidence: This describes specific salt bridges at the luminal entrance.

claims.claim: The cytosolic entrance is lined with salt bridges between the residues R239, D244, R247, R317, E363, K491, and K634.
claims.source: The cytosolic entrance is lined with salt bridges between the residues R239, D244, R247, R317, E363, K491, and K634 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This describes specific salt bridges at the cytosolic entrance.

claims.claim: A portion of CL1 towards the TM2 and C-terminus of the protein is part of the cytosolic entrance of the ACOS.
claims.source: A portion of CL1 towards the TM2 and C-terminus of the protein also seems to be a part of the cytosolic entrance of the ACOS.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural proximity of CL1 to the ACOS.

claims.claim: Sequence conservation between HGSNAT and other known acetyl-CoA binding proteins or transferases is poor.
claims.source: Sequence conservation between HGSNAT and other known acetyl-CoA binding proteins or transferases is poor.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analyses.

claims.claim: There are no structural homologs of HGSNAT.
claims.source: There are no structural homologs of HGSNAT, and a search within the database of known structures using the HGSNAT TMD by the Dali server resulted in hits with sequence identity of <17% across alignments of <25% sequence length (Holm et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural similarity searches using the Dali server.

claims.claim: A search within the database of known structures using the HGSNAT TMD by the Dali server resulted in hits with sequence identity of <17% across alignments of <25% sequence length.
claims.source: There are no structural homologs of HGSNAT, and a search within the database of known structures using the HGSNAT TMD by the Dali server resulted in hits with sequence identity of <17% across alignments of <25% sequence length (Holm et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This describes the results of a structural similarity search.

claims.claim: A search with just the luminal domain yields hits with <15% identity over alignments of at least 70% sequence lengths.
claims.source: Even the search with just the luminal domain, which appeared to be a classic two-sheet β-sandwich, yields hits with <15% identity over alignments of at least 70% sequence lengths (Supplementary file 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This describes the results of a structural similarity search for the LD.

claims.claim: The authors used ModelAngelo, a machine-learning-based de novo automatic model-building algorithm, to build the initial HGSNAT model into the cryo-EM density.
claims.source: We used ModelAngelo, a machine-learning-based de novo automatic model-building algorithm to build the initial HGSNAT model into the cryo-EM density (Jamali et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This describes the computational method used for model building.

claims.claim: The model built by ModelAngelo into the experimental data superposed well with the HGSNAT model as predicted by AlphaFold with a Cα RMSD of ~1.7 Å over 533 amino acids.
claims.source: The model built by ModelAngelo into the experimental data superposed well with the HGSNAT model as predicted by AlphaFold with a Cα RMSD of ~1.7 Å over 533 amino acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This compares the experimental structure with the AlphaFold prediction.

claims.claim: HGSNATs of representatives from archaea, bacteria, and plants suggest that LD and TM1 are absent in other kingdoms.
claims.source: HGSNATs of representatives from archaea, bacteria, and plants suggest that LD and TM1 are absent in other kingdoms.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence and structure comparisons with homologs from other organisms.

claims.claim: HGSNAT homologs from archaea, bacteria, and plants superpose onto the TMD part of HGSNAT, especially TM2-11 with Cα RMSDs of 1–1.4 Å over 350 amino acids.
claims.source: These homologs superpose onto the TMD part of HGSNAT, especially TM2-11 with Cα RMSDs of 1–1.4 Å over 350 amino acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes structural conservation across kingdoms.

claims.claim: The TmAT superfamily of membrane proteins consists of two subfamilies: the acyltransferase-3/acetyl-CoA transporter (ATAT) family (TCDB: 9.B.97) and the integral membrane acetyltransferase (YeiB) family (TCDB: 9.B.169).
claims.source: TmAT superfamily of membrane proteins consists of two subfamilies of integral membrane proteins consisting of 8–12 TMs – the acyltransferase-3/acetyl-CoA transporter (ATAT) family (TCDB: 9.B.97) and the integral membrane acetyltransferase (YeiB) family (TCDB: 9.B.169).
claims.evidence: This describes the classification of the TmAT superfamily.

claims.claim: HGSNAT belongs to the YeiB family.
claims.source: HGSNAT belongs to the YeiB family.
claims.evidence: This classifies HGSNAT within the TmAT superfamily.

claims.claim: A meaningful sequence alignment could not be generated between the members of the ATAT and YeiB families.
claims.source: A meaningful sequence alignment could not be generated between the members of these two families.
claims.evidence: This describes the lack of sequence similarity between the two families.

claims.claim: A bent helix near the predicted acetyl-CoA binding site is observed in the ATAT family, suggesting that this could be a conserved feature amongst the members of the TmAT superfamily.
claims.source: Incidentally, a bent helix near the predicted acetyl-CoA binding site is also observed in the ATAT family, suggesting that this could be a conserved feature amongst the members of the TmAT superfamily (Newman et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison with ATAT family members.

claims.claim: The LD and TM1 regions have poor sequence conservation compared to the rest of the protein.
claims.source: It appears that the LD and TM1 regions have poor sequence conservation compared to the rest of the protein (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: The authors mapped known clinical mutations (missense, nonsense, and polymorphisms) of HGSNAT onto its three-dimensional structure.
claims.source: We mapped the known clinical mutations (missense, nonsense, and polymorphisms) of HGSNAT onto its three-dimensional structure (Canals et al., 2011; Fan et al., 2006; Fedele and Hopwood, 2010; Feldhammer et al., 2009a; Feldhammer et al., 2009b; Hrebícek et al., 2006; Huizing and Gahl, 2020).
claims.evidence: This describes an analysis combining structural and clinical data.

claims.claim: Almost all the mutations fall within the conserved regions on HGSNAT.
claims.source: Almost all the mutations fall within the conserved regions on HGSNAT (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from mapping mutations onto the conservation analysis.

claims.claim: The nonsense mutations seem to be located more on the cytosolic side, and the missense mutations seem to be populated on the luminal side of HGSNAT.
claims.source: The nonsense mutations seem to be located more on the cytosolic side, and the missense mutations seem to be populated on the luminal side of HGSNAT (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from mapping mutations onto the structure.

claims.claim: The authors estimated the extent of destabilization or stabilization introduced by variants on HGSNAT structure using FoldX.
claims.source: We estimated the extent of destabilization or stabilization introduced by these variants on HGSNAT structure by FoldX, a force field algorithm to evaluate the effect of mutations on the stability and dynamics of proteins (Supplementary file 2; Schymkowitz et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This describes a computational analysis of mutation effects.

claims.claim: Most destabilizing mutations appear to be concentrated near the LD-TMD interface.
claims.source: We classified these mutations into four groups based on their position on the structure and found that most destabilizing mutations appear to be concentrated near the LD-TMD interface (Figure 4 and Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the FoldX analysis and structural mapping.

claims.claim: Five missense mutations - E471K (LL3), R344C/R344H (LL2), P283L (TM3), and N258I (TM2) - have been identified in the residues that line the ACOS.
claims.source: Five missense mutations - E471K (LL3), R344C/R344H (LL2), P283L (TM3), and N258I (TM2) - have been identified in the residues that line the ACOS (Figures 4B and 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This lists mutations in the active site region.

claims.claim: E471K mutation could impact the binding affinity of acetyl-CoA because E471 is close to the acetyl group and the mutation changes an acidic to basic side chain.
claims.source: E471 is close to the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA, and acidic to basic side chain substitution in an E471K mutation could impact the binding affinity of acetyl-CoA.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the effect of the mutation based on the structure.

claims.claim: N258I mutation could directly impact the binding of acetyl-CoA and acetyltransferase activity because N258 is hydrogen bonded to acetyl-CoA.
claims.source: N258 side chain can act as both hydrogen acceptor or donor and is hydrogen bonded to acetyl-CoA in the structure. N258I mutation could directly impact the binding of acetyl-CoA and acetyltransferase activity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the effect of the mutation based on the structure.

claims.claim: R344C/R344H mutations could affect the integrity of the luminal entrance of ACOS because R344 forms salt bridges with E469 and E471 that stabilize the luminal entrance.
claims.source: R344 forms salt bridges with E469 and E471 that stabilize the luminal entrance of ACOS. The mutations of R344C/R344H could affect the integrity of the luminal entrance of ACOS.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the effect of the mutations based on the structure.

claims.claim: P283L mutation could alter the TM3 conformation on the luminal side and thus affect acetyl-CoA binding.
claims.source: P283 is not directly involved in the binding of acetyl-CoA. However, the residues flanking P283 – V281, F282, F285, I288, and M289 – all interact with the pantothenate group of acetyl-CoA (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). Proline residues define helix conformation, and mutation of a relatively conserved proline to an aliphatic leucine could alter the TM3 conformation on the luminal side and thus affect acetyl-CoA binding.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the effect of the mutation based on structural considerations.

claims.claim: FoldX prediction indicates that P283L is the most destabilizing of all ACOS mutations.
claims.source: FoldX prediction indicates that P283L is the most destabilizing of all ACOS mutations perhaps because it impacts the TM3 conformation.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the FoldX computational analysis.

claims.claim: N258I and R344H substitutions did not reduce the overall expression of HGSNAT.
claims.source: We generated N258I and R344H mutants to test the effect of these substitutions on the expression and stability of HGSNAT. We noticed that these substitutions did not reduce the overall expression of HGSNAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation about mutant expression.

claims.claim: R344H mutant showed slightly enhanced aggregation upon solubilization in 1% digitonin but the overall stability was not drastically altered compared to WT HGSNAT.
claims.source: R344H mutant, upon solubilization in 1% digitonin, showed slightly enhanced aggregation but the overall stability of R344H mutant was not altered drastically, compared to WT HGSNAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and I, and 1 L).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation about the R344H mutant.

claims.claim: Although the N258I mutant showed expression comparable to WT HGSNAT, no peak for N258I nor free GFP could be observed in FSEC.
claims.source: Although the N258I mutant showed expression comparable to WT HGSNAT, as evident by total fluorescence measurements of solubilized cell lysates, we could not observe any peak for N258I nor free GFP in FSEC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation about the N258I mutant.

claims.claim: N258I substitution directly affected the substrate binding and stability, resulting in the unstable protein being pelleted out of solution upon solubilization followed by ultracentrifugation.
claims.source: We hypothesize that N258I substitution directly affected the substrate binding and stability. As a result, upon solubilization followed by ultracentrifugation, the unstable protein got pelleted out of the solution (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the experimental observations for N258I.

claims.claim: C76F, G262R, N273K, G423W, and G424S/G424V are all missense mutations that are on the LD-TMD interface.
claims.source: C76F, G262R, N273K, G423W, and G424S/G424V are all missense mutations that are on the LD-TMD interface, and our FoldX-based analysis indicates these mutations to be the most destabilizing among the ones that we listed.

results.result: The authors determined the first high-resolution cryo-EM structure of HGSNAT in complex with acetyl-CoA at 3.26 Å global resolution, revealing that HGSNAT is a dimer with C2 symmetry and comprises an N-terminal luminal domain (LD) and 11 transmembrane helices (TMs) per protomer.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C60-C66 describe the structure determination and overall architecture, supported by cryo-EM data (Table 1, Figures 1-3). The resolution, symmetry, domain organization, and completeness of the model are well-documented. C131-C132 show agreement between the experimental structure and AlphaFold predictions (RMSD ~1.7 Å), providing independent validation. The claim of novelty (C62, C42) is verifiable through structural database searches.

results.result: The transmembrane domain exhibits a novel 4+4 fold architecture with internal pseudo-symmetry, where TMs 2-5 and TMs 6-9 are related by twofold rotation, forming a 'catalytic core' (TMs 2-5, TM10) and 'scaffold domain' (TMs 6-9, TM11), designated as the TNAT fold.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C74 describe the TMD architecture based on structural analysis (Figure 1D-F). The internal symmetry, domain organization, and evolutionary conservation (C73) are supported by structural data and sequence analysis. The naming of the TNAT fold (C74) is justified by the novelty of the architecture. However, the functional designation of 'catalytic core' and 'scaffold domain' is partly inferential based on proximity to the active site.

results.result: The luminal domain is a ~110 amino acid β-sandwich with a novel 'transthyretin-like' fold, comprising two β-sheets with unusual strand topology, positioned ~45 Å from the dimer interface and not involved in dimerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C84 describe the LD structure based on cryo-EM density (Figure 1, 2). The β-sandwich architecture, strand arrangement, and disulfide bonds are directly observed. C130, C214-C215 show that structural similarity searches yield <15% identity hits, supporting the novelty claim. The classification as 'transthyretin-like' is based on comparative analysis, though the fold is distinct enough to be considered novel. The lower resolution of LD (C61, C84) is acknowledged.

results.result: The LD-TMD interface is stabilized by an extensive ~35 Å interaction network involving salt bridges, hydrogen bonds, and hydrophobic interactions, which is essential for protein folding and stability as demonstrated by the C76F mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C95 describe specific interactions at the LD-TMD interface observed in the structure (Figure 2B, Figure 2—supplement 2A). The interactions are well-documented with specific residues identified. C158 provides experimental validation: the C76F mutation at this interface reduces protein expression, supporting the functional importance of these interactions. The combination of structural and mutational data strongly supports this result.

results.result: The dimer interface spans ~35 Å on the luminal side, primarily mediated by a C334-C334 disulfide bond between LL2 loops and extensive π-π interactions between LL2 and LL5, with the C334A mutant converting to monomer upon heating while F593A remains stable.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C104 describe the dimer interface structure (Figure 2C, Figure 2—supplement 2B). C105-C110 provide experimental validation through mutagenesis: C334A disrupts the disulfide and becomes monomeric upon heating, while F593A remains dimeric, demonstrating the critical role of the C334-C334 disulfide. The extensive π-π network provides additional stability at room temperature. The experimental and structural data are mutually consistent and well-documented (Figure 4—supplement 1).

results.result: The acetyl-CoA binding site (ACOS) is a ~75 Å pore spanning the TMD, lined by conserved residues of TMs 2-5 and bent TM10, with endogenously bound acetyl-CoA positioned such that its nucleoside head faces the cytosol and acetyl group is hydrogen-bonded to N258, ~4.5 Å from catalytic H269.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C125 describe the ACOS structure based on MOLEonline prediction and cryo-EM density (Figure 3, Figure 3—supplement 1). The acetyl-CoA position, orientation, and interactions are clearly resolved in the density. C163 provides independent validation through LC-MS confirmation of endogenously bound acetyl-CoA. The TM10 bend (C113-C114) is structurally characterized. The charge polarity (C120) and specific interactions (C116, C122-C125) are well-documented. The mean correlation coefficient of 0.77 for acetyl-CoA modeling supports the quality of the fit.

results.result: Mapping of >70 known MPS IIIC mutations onto the structure reveals that most destabilizing mutations cluster at the LD-TMD interface, with catalytic core mutations (E471K, R344C/H, P283L, N258I) directly affecting acetyl-CoA binding, as validated by N258I complete destabilization and R344H mild aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C144 describe the mutation mapping and FoldX analysis (Figure 4, Supplementary file 2). C145-C150 identify specific catalytic core mutations and predict their effects based on structural analysis. C151-C154 provide experimental validation: N258I shows complete destabilization (no FSEC peak despite expression), while R344H shows mild aggregation but maintained stability. The structural predictions are consistent with experimental observations. However, the mechanistic explanations (C146-C149) are inferences from structure, not direct functional measurements.

results.result: LD-TMD interface mutations (C76F, G262R, N273K, G423W, G424S/V) are predicted by FoldX to be highly destabilizing, with C76F experimentally confirmed to reduce protein expression, demonstrating the importance of LD-TMD interactions for folding.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C157 describe FoldX predictions for LD-TMD interface mutations (Figure 4, Supplementary file 2). C158 provides experimental validation: C76F reduces expression (Figure 4—supplement 1A,B), supporting the prediction and demonstrating functional importance. The combination of computational prediction and experimental validation is consistent. However, only one mutation (C76F) was experimentally tested, limiting the validation of other predictions.

results.result: Scaffold domain mutations (W403C, M482K, G486E, A489E, S518F, S539C, S541L) are predicted to be only mildly destabilizing, with W403C experimentally showing reduced thermal stability but maintained expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C160 describe FoldX predictions for scaffold domain mutations. C161 provides experimental validation for W403C: expression is maintained but thermal stability is reduced (Figure 4—supplement 1A,G,I,M), consistent with the 'mildly destabilizing' prediction. The structural rationale (mutations face away from protein core) is reasonable. However, only one mutation was experimentally tested.

results.result: The structure represents an acetyl-CoA primed state at pH 7.5 where H269 is uncharged and acetyl-CoA is held by N258, awaiting protonation of H269 and substrate binding for catalysis, with N258 playing a greater role in stability than H269 as shown by complete destabilization of N258I versus stable H269A.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C174 describe the interpretation of the structural state based on pH, acetyl-CoA binding, and prior biochemical data (C164-C167). C175-C177 provide experimental validation: H269A maintains expression and stability while N258I is completely destabilized, supporting the greater role of N258 in acetyl-CoA binding and protein stability. The interpretation is consistent with the structural observations (C172) and biochemical principles (C170-C171). However, the mechanistic interpretation (C173-C174) involves inference beyond direct structural observation.

results.result: Evolutionary analysis reveals that the TMD (TMs 2-11) is highly conserved across kingdoms (RMSD 1-1.4 Å with archaea, bacteria, plants), while LD and TM1 are metazoan-specific, suggesting LD+TM1 form α-HGSNAT and TMs 2-11 form β-HGSNAT.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C134 show structural conservation of TMD across kingdoms with low RMSDs (Figure 2—supplement 1). C73, C139 show TMD is evolutionarily conserved while LD/TM1 are not (Figure 4A). C211-C213 describe the genomic organization supporting this division. The speculation about α/β-HGSNAT boundaries (C213) is based on multiple lines of evidence (evolutionary conservation, genomic organization, structural flexibility). However, C87 shows the recombinant protein is not proteolyzed, so the α/β division is inferred rather than directly observed.

results.result: The structure does not definitively resolve the catalytic mechanism debate, as the acetyl-CoA bound conformation could proceed through ordered sequential, random sequential, or ping-pong mechanisms, and concurrent work by Xu et al. also does not resolve substrate binding order or disprove acetylated intermediates.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-C194, C226 acknowledge limitations of the current structure in resolving mechanistic questions. C197 critically assesses concurrent work. This is an honest assessment supported by the structural data showing only one state (acetyl-CoA bound) without evidence of H269 acetylation (C190) or substrate-bound states. The structure provides a snapshot but not a complete mechanistic picture. This limitation is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Optimization of HGSNAT expression and purification identified digitonin as the optimal detergent, with the protein predominantly dimeric in most conditions and best expressed at 32°C post-transduction, using N-terminal GFP fusion based on ColabFold predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C59 describe systematic optimization of expression and purification conditions using FSEC (Figure 1—supplement 1). The experimental approach is sound: testing GFP position (C51), temperature (C55), detergent screening (C56), and thermal stability (C57). The choice of N-terminal GFP (C53) is rationalized by ColabFold prediction (C52). The observations are well-documented with supporting figures. This represents solid biochemical optimization work.

results.result: HGSNAT shows poor sequence conservation with known acetyl-CoA binding proteins and no structural homologs (Dali hits <17% identity over <25% length), belonging to the YeiB family of the TmAT superfamily, with a bent helix near the acetyl-CoA binding site potentially conserved across TmAT members.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C130 describe lack of homology based on sequence and structure searches (Supplementary file 1). C135-C137 classify HGSNAT within TmAT superfamily. C138 notes a potentially conserved feature (bent helix) across families. The searches are appropriately conducted and the lack of homology supports the novelty claim. The classification is based on database annotations. The bent helix observation (C138) is speculative but reasonable based on cited work on ATAT family.

results.result: The function of the luminal domain remains unknown, though DeepSite predicts a ligand binding site and it may bind heparan sulfate to position the substrate near the active site, potentially undergoing conformational changes similar to SGNH domains in related proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C216-C223 acknowledge the unknown function of LD and present speculations. C217 describes a computational prediction (DeepSite). C219-C220 note lipid enhancement and unexplained density. C221-C222 draw analogies to OafB. C223 speculates about HS binding. These are reasonable hypotheses but lack experimental validation. The speculation is appropriately presented as such, but without functional data, the LD function remains uncertain.

results.result: Prior biochemical studies proposed conflicting mechanisms: Rome et al. suggested a ping-pong mechanism with histidine acetylation, Pshezhetsky et al. supported acetylated intermediates, Meikle et al. argued for random-order ternary complex formation, while Mahuran et al. found no acetylated intermediate.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C189 accurately summarize prior biochemical work with appropriate citations. This represents a fair assessment of the conflicting literature on HGSNAT mechanism. The authors correctly identify the key debates in the field. This background is important for contextualizing their structural findings and acknowledging that the structure alone does not resolve these debates.

results.result: The proteolytic processing of HGSNAT into α and β subunits remains unclear, with the proposed C123-C434 disulfide impossible in the current structure (~34 Å apart), and the recombinant protein appearing non-proteolyzed, suggesting α/β subunits are held together by non-covalent interactions rather than disulfides.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 describe prior knowledge about proteolytic processing. C87, C210 show the recombinant protein is not proteolyzed. C201-C204 demonstrate the proposed C123-C434 disulfide is structurally impossible in this conformation. C202-C203 identify alternative disulfide partners. C205-C209 discuss uncertainty about protease sites. The structural evidence contradicts a prior proposal (C123-C434 disulfide) and the authors appropriately propose alternative explanations (C205). However, the non-proteolyzed recombinant protein limits direct insights into the mature form.

results.result: Concurrent work by Xu et al. obtained structures at pH 8.0 in GDN showing limited conformational changes, but future structures at lysosomal pH in membrane mimetics with native lipids are needed to fully resolve the catalytic mechanism and potential pH-driven conformational changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C195-C197 accurately describe concurrent work and its limitations. C198-C200 propose future experiments needed to resolve mechanistic questions. This represents appropriate acknowledgment of concurrent work and honest assessment of what remains unknown. The suggestions for future work (lysosomal pH, membrane mimetics, native lipids) are reasonable based on the current limitations.

results.result: The authors determined the first high-resolution cryo-EM structure of HGSNAT in complex with acetyl-CoA at 3.26 Å resolution, representing the first experimentally determined structure of any member of the transmembrane acyl transferase (TmAT) superfamily.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm the structural work as 'convincing' with 'high resolution and isotropic single-particle cryoEM map' and 'high-quality' density. One reviewer states 'This is the first structure of any member of the transmembrane acyl transferase superfamily' and notes the density for acetyl-CoA is 'particularly well-defined.' The editors describe this as an 'important study' providing 'the first description of the architecture of this family.'

results.result: The structure reveals HGSNAT is a dimer with C2 symmetry, where each protomer contains an N-terminal luminal domain and 11 transmembrane helices organized into a catalytic core (TMs 2-5, TM10) and scaffold domain (TMs 6-9, TM11), representing a novel 'transmembrane N-acetyltransferase (TNAT) fold.'
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm the architectural findings. One reviewer states the authors 'show that the protein is a dimer, and define the architecture of the alpha- and beta-GSNAT fragments' and that the work 'provides important insights into the architecture.' Another notes the authors 'thoroughly describe the architecture of HGSNAT.' No concerns are raised about these structural observations.

results.result: The structure reveals the acetyl-CoA binding site with the nucleoside head group toward the cytosol and the acetyl group hydrogen-bonded to N258, with the catalytic H269 positioned ~4.5 Å from the acetyl group at the luminal entrance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the acetyl-CoA binding characterization. One states 'the density for the acetyl-CoA ligand is particularly well-defined, as are the contacting residues within the transmembrane domain.' The editors note the work 'reveals the mode of acetyl-CoA binding' with 'strong density for the acetyl-CoA ligand.' The structural data for ligand binding is consistently described as convincing.

results.result: The dimer interface is stabilized primarily by a C334-C334 disulfide bond between protomers and extensive π-π interactions between aromatic residues of LL2 and LL5. Mutagenesis shows C334A disrupts the dimer upon heating while F593A does not affect dimer stability.
results.evaluation: The structural characterization of the dimer interface is accepted by reviewers as part of the overall high-quality structural work. The mutagenesis experiments (C334A, F593A) are presented as supporting data but are not specifically critiqued by reviewers, suggesting implicit acceptance as consistent with the structural observations.

results.result: The authors mapped known MPS IIIC mutations onto the structure and used FoldX to predict their destabilizing effects, identifying mutations in the active site (E471K, R344C/H, P283L, N258I) and at the LD-TMD interface as most destabilizing.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the mutation mapping ('map the mutations known to cause MPS IIIC') but express concern about incomplete experimental validation. The editors state 'experimental support for...the impact of disease-causing mutations is incomplete.' One reviewer notes the study 'outline[s] a catalytic mechanism' and 'propose[s] potential reasons why certain human mutations lead to lysosomal storage disorders' through 'careful structural analysis,' but the lack of functional validation creates uncertainty about the mechanistic interpretations.

results.result: Experimental characterization of selected mutants (N258I, R344H, C76F, W403C) shows varying effects on expression and stability, with N258I causing complete destabilization and C76F reducing expression, supporting predictions about the importance of substrate binding and the LD-TMD interface.
results.evaluation: While the mutant characterization data is presented, reviewers express concern about the lack of functional activity measurements. One reviewer explicitly requests: 'The authors should characterize whether the purified protein is active' and suggests 'at the very least, the authors should try a cell-based assay to demonstrate that the GFP tag does not interfere with the function.' Another reviewer notes 'A weakness of the study is the lack of functional validation. The enzymatic activity of the enzyme characterized was not measured.' This makes the mechanistic interpretations of mutant effects uncertain.

results.result: The authors interpret the structure as representing an acetyl-CoA-primed state waiting for H269 protonation and substrate binding, and discuss how it relates to three possible catalytic mechanisms (Ping Pong Bi Bi, Random Bi Bi, Ordered Bi Bi), though the structure does not definitively resolve the mechanism.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express significant concern about the mechanistic interpretations. One reviewer states: 'In Figure 5, the authors present a detailed schematic of the catalytic cycle, which I find to be too speculative. There is no evidence to suggest that this enzyme undergoes isomerization, similar to a transporter, between open-to-lumen and open-to-cytosol states.' The editors note 'experimental support for the molecular mechanism of the HS acetylation reaction...is incomplete.' The authors themselves acknowledge 'The structure that we obtained does not by itself settle the debate about the mechanism.'

results.result: LC-MS analysis confirmed the presence of endogenously bound acetyl-CoA in the purified protein, demonstrating tight binding that persisted through purification without exogenous addition.
results.evaluation: This biochemical characterization supports the structural observation of acetyl-CoA binding and is not questioned by reviewers. It provides important context for interpreting the structure, though reviewers do not specifically comment on this finding.

results.result: The recombinant HGSNAT used for structure determination is a non-proteolyzed form, as evidenced by SDS-PAGE and FSEC analysis showing full-length protein.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly raises concern: 'the enzyme lacks native proteolytic processing, so it is a little unclear whether the structure represents an active enzyme.' This creates uncertainty about whether the structural state observed is physiologically relevant, though the high-quality structural data itself is not questioned.

results.result: The luminal domain (LD) is a ~110 amino acid β-sandwich with a novel fold best described as 'transthyretin-like,' containing two predicted disulfide bonds though only C76-C79 could be unambiguously modeled.
results.evaluation: The structural characterization of the LD is accepted as part of the overall high-quality structural work. Reviewers note the 'density map is of high-quality, except for the luminal domain,' acknowledging the lower resolution in this region but not questioning the overall architectural description.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the overall structure determination and novelty claims (C9, C60, C62). OpenEval emphasizes cryo-EM resolution, AlphaFold validation, and structural database searches. Peer reviewers describe the work as 'convincing' with 'high-quality' density and affirm this as 'the first structure of any member of the transmembrane acyl transferase superfamily.'

Both support the TMD architecture findings (C68, C69, C71, C74). OpenEval notes the internal symmetry and TNAT fold naming, with some inference about functional designations. Peer reviewers affirm the authors 'thoroughly describe the architecture of HGSNAT' and 'define the architecture' without raising concerns about these structural observations.

Both support the LD structural characterization (C78-C84, C130, C214-C215). OpenEval emphasizes the β-sandwich architecture, novelty based on structural searches, and acknowledges lower resolution. Peer reviewers accept the LD description as part of 'high-quality' structural work while noting 'density map is of high-quality, except for the luminal domain.'

Both support the acetyl-CoA binding characterization (C115-C117). OpenEval describes the ACOS structure with MOLEonline prediction, cryo-EM density, and LC-MS validation (C163). Peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'the density for the acetyl-CoA ligand is particularly well-defined, as are the contacting residues' and describe it as 'convincing.'

Both support the dimer interface structural characterization (C98-C99, C105-C110). OpenEval emphasizes the C334-C334 disulfide validation through mutagenesis experiments showing C334A becomes monomeric while F593A remains dimeric. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of the overall high-quality structural work without specific critique.

Both address disease mutation mapping (C140-C150) but with different levels of certainty. OpenEval finds the FoldX analysis and limited experimental validation (N258I, R344H) supportive, noting mechanistic explanations are inferences. Peer reviewers acknowledge the mutation mapping but express concern about 'incomplete experimental validation' and lack of functional data, creating uncertainty about mechanistic interpretations.

Both address LD-TMD interface mutations (C155-C158), with OpenEval finding C76F validation supportive but noting limited testing. Peer reviewers group this with broader concerns about incomplete functional validation, requesting activity measurements and cell-based assays to demonstrate the GFP tag doesn't interfere with function.

Both address scaffold domain mutations (C159-C161). OpenEval finds W403C validation consistent with predictions. Peer reviewers express broader uncertainty due to lack of functional activity measurements, with one explicitly stating 'A weakness of the study is the lack of functional validation.'

Both address mechanistic interpretation (C173-C174) but with different assessments. OpenEval finds the interpretation consistent with structural observations and biochemical principles, though acknowledging inference beyond direct observation. Peer reviewers express significant concern, with one stating the catalytic cycle schematic is 'too speculative' with 'no evidence to suggest that this enzyme undergoes isomerization.'

Both address limitations in resolving mechanistic questions (C193-C194). OpenEval views the authors' acknowledgment of limitations as appropriate and honest. Peer reviewers similarly note 'experimental support for the molecular mechanism...is incomplete' and cite the authors' own statement that 'The structure...does not by itself settle the debate about the mechanism.'

Both address the lack of proteolytic processing (C87, C210). OpenEval notes this limits direct insights into the mature form but finds the structural evidence about disulfide bonds valuable. Peer reviewers express concern that 'the enzyme lacks native proteolytic processing, so it is a little unclear whether the structure represents an active enzyme.'

OpenEval finds the LD-TMD interface interactions (C89-C95) well-documented with C76F mutation providing experimental validation. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though this overlaps with broader mutation validation concerns addressed in R6.

OpenEval supports the evolutionary conservation analysis of TMD across kingdoms (C133-C134, C73, C139, C211-C213) with structural and genomic evidence. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports the systematic optimization of expression and purification using FSEC (C50-C59), describing it as 'solid biochemical optimization work.' No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports the lack of homology findings (C127-C130) and TmAT superfamily classification (C135-C138) based on sequence and structure searches. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval rates LD function speculation (C216-C223) as uncertain, noting reasonable hypotheses lack experimental validation. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though reviewers generally accept the structural characterization of LD.

OpenEval supports the summary of prior biochemical work (C178-C189) as accurate and fair assessment of conflicting literature. Peer reviewers reference this background (C182, C186) in context of mechanistic uncertainty but don't specifically evaluate the literature summary.
OpenEval supports the authors' assessment of concurrent work limitations and proposed future experiments (C195-C200). No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found.

Peer reviewers support the LC-MS confirmation of endogenously bound acetyl-CoA (C163, C191) as biochemical characterization consistent with structural observations. OpenEval addresses C163 within R6 and R10 as validation for structural findings but doesn't separately evaluate C191.
